revisions.title: From erotic pursuit to a qualified superlative
revisions.body: The opening frames Socrates as hunting Alcibiades, then undercuts that erotic premise: he says he forgot the youth and redirects beauty’s measure toward wisdom. Protagoras is introduced not simply as the wisest man Socrates has met, but—subject to agreement—as the wisest among those now living. One way to hear that qualification is as a restraint on the superlative: the claim is bounded by the present generation and offered for the companion’s assent.

revisions.title: Before buying wisdom, name its object
revisions.body: Socrates turns Hippocrates’ urgency into a test of intelligibility. One way to read the passage is that desire must name its object before it spends money or entrusts a soul: “sophist” may announce a purchase without explaining its promise. The opening exchange prepares this pressure. Socrates recasts excitement as a possible wrong and answers it with money and a remedy; Hippocrates’ laughter marks the mismatch (obs_protagoras_0006). The scene delays judgment on Protagoras and questions the buyer’s readiness.

revisions.title: Learning enters the soul
revisions.body: Socrates makes learning dangerous by removing the distance between purchase and use. Food can remain outside the body for inspection; a lesson cannot remain outside the soul. Once paid for, it enters the soul through learning, so the buyer leaves either harmed or helped. Read this as a warning about intellectual custody: judgment must precede absorption, not follow it.

revisions.title: Protagoras chooses disclosure
revisions.body: The key turn in this unit is Protagoras’s proposed strategy of visibility. He describes sophistry as an old practice that earlier practitioners hid behind poetry, rites, athletics, or music, then says he will instead admit the name. That is a position he advances, not settled history: the passage reports his account and Socrates’ dispute with it.

revisions.title: The question before the demonstration
revisions.body: Socrates turns Protagoras’s promise of daily improvement into a demand for a domain: unlike painting or flute-playing, what exactly will Hippocrates learn? Protagoras answers with euboulia for managing a household and presents his undertaking as political craft that makes good citizens. The section stops at the problem, not its solution: Socrates asks whether this civic excellence is teachable, and Protagoras is called on to demonstrate it.

revisions.title: Two distributions, one city
revisions.body: The myth invites a distinction between two distributions. Epimetheus assigns protective capacities by compensating among kinds, while Prometheus gives humans technical wisdom but not the political art. Zeus’s later remedy is different: respect and right must be shared by everyone, because a city cannot exist if only a few possess them. The point I take is that the story shifts the question from who has a skill to what all must share for a city to exist.

revisions.title: From myth to logos: punishment as evidence
revisions.body: Do not hear the transition as a turn from myth to punishment. Protagoras explicitly says that he will now offer a logos rather than a mythos; punishment belongs inside that argument as its evidence. His point is that reasoned punishment looks forward—to deter repetition and educate—so he presents the practice as evidence that virtue can be taught.

revisions.title: When everyone is already a teacher
revisions.body: Protagoras shifts the problem from finding a single source of virtue to recognizing a distributed civic formation. His analogy with craftsmen’s sons suggests that people already acquire a practice through family and fellow practitioners; virtue likewise belongs to a community in which everyone teaches as far as he can. The specialist is not thereby unnecessary, but his advantage is harder to isolate: he is the one who advances someone even a little.

revisions.title: The parts model under pressure
revisions.body: Here the dialogue shifts from virtue’s teachability to the structure of virtue itself. Protagoras proposes a face-parts model: justice, temperance, holiness, and the rest are distinct parts, each with its own power. Socrates tests that model through self-predication: justice is just, and holiness is holy. He then presses the relation between those terms, saying justice and holiness are either the same or most similar. Protagoras resists that easy identification and insists that a difference remains.

revisions.title: Who sets the terms of speech?
revisions.body: Socrates turns brevity into a condition of dialogue: Protagoras must speak in a way Socrates can follow, or Socrates will leave. Protagoras answers by tying his reputation to resisting an opponent’s control of the format. When Callias physically holds Socrates back, a dispute about conversational procedure becomes the immediate drama of the gathering.

revisions.title: From Simonides’ refutation to a new exposition
revisions.body: Socrates’ reading makes the poem a contest with Pittacus: Simonides shifts the problem from being good to becoming good, then says that remaining good is impossible for a human being. That argument does not end by returning to the agreed exchange. As I hear 347a, it ends in a handoff: Socrates states his view, and Hippias offers another elegant exposition. The point is not closure but a fresh claim on the floor.

revisions.title: The inquiry returns to the speakers
revisions.body: The hinge of this section is methodological, not yet doctrinal. Socrates sets poetry aside and proposes that the speakers test truth directly; then he restates the five-part virtue question as an open disjunction. Hear the reset clearly: the issue is no longer what a poet can be made to mean, but whether Protagoras’s own account can withstand examination.

revisions.title: The closing audit
revisions.body: Socrates makes the ending an audit of the argument: his opening denial that virtue is teachable now collides with the route that makes justice, moderation, and courage knowledge, while Protagoras’s original thesis appears to point toward the opposite result. He proposes a sequence, not a reset: establish what virtue is, then revisit teachability. Prometheus names his preference for forethought in inquiry; Protagoras defers the matter, and they depart.
